ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Psychiatry Consultation — Martin Luther King Jr.

code.originalText: Two-week review and psychiatry consultation: diagnosis, safety, therapy and medicine

text.paragraph: Exhaustion, broken sleep and low mood for about two months in a 36-year-old minister and civil rights leader who lives under sustained, real threat and works without rest. Please confirm the diagnosis (depression, an adjustment disorder, PTSD or an insomnia disorder), review his safety, and advise on therapy and medicine in a way that protects his privacy. [S]

list.item: Does he have major depressive disorder, an adjustment disorder, or another condition?
Does he have PTSD, given the stabbing, the bombing and the continuing threats, or is his vigilance proportionate to real danger?
How should his suicide risk be understood, given the childhood act of self-injury, the anonymous letter and his expectation of being killed?
What treatment do you recommend: psychotherapy, an antidepressant, or both, and how should his insomnia be treated?
Is varenicline safe for him to stop smoking alongside treatment for depression, and when should it start?
How can his care respect his faith, his privacy under surveillance and his experience of racism, and what work changes would help?

text.paragraph: Dr. King, 36, is seen at the request of Dr. Ashby-Nwankwo. For about two months, after a winter of continuous campaigning and an admission for exhaustion six months ago, he has had low mood most days, loss of pleasure in reading and preaching, guilt that he cannot do more, poor concentration, fatigue and broken sleep of about five hours, with an hour to fall asleep and waking before five. His energy returns on the platform but drains afterwards. He has lived for nearly ten years with threats against his life and his family, including the bombing of his home, a stabbing that required chest surgery, jailings, and anonymous threats, one of which urged him to take his own life; he believes his calls are monitored. He is watchful in crowds and at home, but has no nightmares, flashbacks, avoidance or emotional numbing. He has never had a period of elevated mood, high energy or little need for sleep. At twelve, grieving his grandmother, he impulsively injured himself; he has not had thoughts of suicide since and has none now. He speaks calmly of the likelihood that he will be killed. His faith, his family and his congregation sustain him. He fears that a psychiatric record could be used against him and his work. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: He was born Michael King on January 15, 1929, at 501 Auburn Avenue in Atlanta, Georgia. [D]

In 1934 his father, the Reverend Michael King, attended the Baptist World Alliance meeting in Berlin and afterwards changed his own name and his son's from Michael to Martin Luther, after the German Protestant reformer; the son's birth certificate was altered to read Martin Luther King, Jr. on July 23, 1957. [D]

His grandmother, Jennie Celeste Williams, died on May 18, 1941, when he was twelve, while he was at a parade without his parents' permission. Grieved and remorseful, he reacted with an impulsive act of self-injury at home. The editors of his papers note that neither he nor his father later described this as a suicide attempt; his father wrote that he cried off and on for several days and could not sleep at night. [D]

He entered Morehouse College in 1944, was ordained in 1948, graduated from Crozer Theological Seminary in 1951, and received his doctorate in systematic theology from Boston University on June 5, 1955. [D]
He married Coretta Scott on June 18, 1953, at the Scott home near Marion, Alabama. [D]

As president of the Montgomery Improvement Association during the bus boycott, his home was bombed on the evening of January 30, 1956, while he spoke at a mass meeting; his wife and daughter were not hurt, and he pleaded with an angry crowd for nonviolence. [D]

On September 20, 1958, at a book signing at Blumstein's Department Store in Harlem, he was stabbed in the upper left side of the chest with a seven-inch steel letter opener. At Harlem Hospital he had more than two hours of surgery; the blade lay so close to the aorta that, he was told, a sneeze could have punctured it, and he wrote that his whole chest had to be opened to remove it. He left the hospital on October 3 and convalesced until late October. [D]

He was arrested and jailed repeatedly: at a sit-in at Rich's department store in Atlanta in October 1960, when he was sentenced to four months of hard labor for violating probation; in Albany, Georgia, in December 1961 and in July 1962, when he spent two weeks in jail; and in Birmingham from April 12 to 19, 1963. [D]

The FBI monitored him from December 1955; wiretaps on his home and the SCLC offices were authorized in October 1963, and he was subjected to surveillance under the counterintelligence program. In about November 1964 the FBI anonymously sent him a recording with an anonymous letter that SCLC staff read as urging him to take his own life. [D]

In October 1964, exhausted by a heavy speaking schedule and with a respiratory infection, he was admitted to St. Joseph's Infirmary in Atlanta for several days of rest; he was asleep there on October 14, 1964, when his wife telephoned to tell him he had been awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. [D]
He received the Nobel Peace Prize in Oslo on December 10, 1964, at 35 the youngest person to have won it. [D]
After voting rights marchers were beaten at the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma on March 7, 1965, he led the march from Selma to Montgomery from March 17 to 25, 1965. [D]
A man who drove for the King family in the mid-1960s described him as a chain smoker who kept his cigarettes hidden at home. [D]

Biographers and historians describe depression in his adult life: David Garrow wrote that, partly as a result of the FBI's intimidation, he often suffered from morbid depression, a contention others have disputed; a psychologist writing in 2024 states that, although never diagnosed, he had serious bouts of depression that he kept secret for fear it could be used against him. [R]

list.item: Major depressive disorder, single episode, moderate (DSM-5-TR) (F32.1). He has five or more DSM-5-TR symptoms, including depressed mood and loss of interest, for more than two weeks, with impairment, so this is major depression and not an adjustment disorder, which cannot be diagnosed when the criteria for another disorder are met. Severity is moderate. There is no history of hypomania and the MDQ is negative, so an antidepressant is appropriate. Threat, surveillance, racism and overwork are causes of the episode, not personal failings, and are recorded as psychosocial factors. [S]

PTSD considered. He was exposed to traumatic events, but he has no intrusion or avoidance symptoms, and his vigilance is proportionate to a real and continuing danger. PTSD criteria are not met; PC-PTSD-5 2 agrees. Screening should be repeated, because symptoms can emerge later. [S]

Suicide risk. No current suicidal ideation, intent, plan or preparatory behavior. The impulsive act in childhood grief, the letter urging suicide, depression and insomnia raise risk; his faith, purpose, family, congregation and engagement in care are strong protective factors. His expectation of being killed is a realistic appraisal of danger, not passive suicidal ideation, and should be distinguished from it at each review. Overall risk is low; outpatient care with the safety plan is appropriate. [S]

Insomnia disorder, comorbid with depression (G47.00). Insomnia on most nights for more than three months with daytime impairment, driven by late-night work, travel and hyperarousal. Sleep apnea is unlikely. CBT for insomnia is the first-line treatment; a hypnotic is not advised. [S]

Smoking cessation during depression treatment (F17.210). Stopping smoking does not worsen depression and often improves mood. In the EAGLES trial varenicline did not significantly increase serious neuropsychiatric events in smokers with psychiatric disorders, and it was the most effective option. Starting it a few weeks after sertraline lets side effects be told apart. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Ashby-Nwankwo's intake note and tests: PHQ-9 17 with item 9 scored 0, GAD-7 11, PC-PTSD-5 2, AUDIT-C 2; blood count, metabolic panel, TSH and hemoglobin A1c normal; ECG normal with QTc 412 ms. Today's PHQ-9 16 and his two-week sleep diary (about five hours a night). Mood Disorder Questionnaire today negative. Insomnia Severity Index 18; STOP-Bang 2. [S]

list.item: Weekly cognitive behavioral therapy with behavioral activation and CBT for insomnia, with a therapist of his choosing who will work with his faith; then every two weeks once he responds, and monthly in remission. [S]
Sertraline 25 mg each morning for a week, then 50 mg; tolerability check by telephone two weeks after starting; increase only if the PHQ-9 has not fallen by about eight to twelve weeks. [S]
CBT for insomnia: fixed rising time, a sleep window widened as sleep improves, no work in bed, no tobacco or coffee in the evening; no hypnotic. [S]
PHQ-9 at every visit; suicide risk reassessed at every visit, distinguishing expectation of being killed from a wish to die; PC-PTSD-5 again at about three months. [S]
Varenicline with counseling, starting about three weeks after sertraline, with a quit date a week later and mood watched. [S]
A sustainable work plan: a full day off each week, no more than two speeches a day, delegation of travel and correspondence, and a two-week break in the summer. [S]
Privacy: restricted chart, documentation limited to what care requires, and secure video for follow-up. [S]
Psychiatry review by video at about eight to twelve weeks, sooner if needed. [S]

Discussed with Dr. Ashby-Nwankwo, who saw him the same day. The diagnosis, the reasons PTSD is not diagnosed, the safety assessment and the options were explained to Dr. King, who chose therapy and sertraline and agreed to the work plan. [S]
Follow-up: Psychiatry review by video in about eight to twelve weeks; therapy weekly. [S]
